22.title: Born at Talwandi, 1469
22.hook: Nanak is born to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta in a Punjab village now called Nankana Sahib
22.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's birth each year, usually at the full moon of Kartik in the autumn, with processions, continuous readings of the scripture, kirtan and langar; many make pilgrimage to Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Camp one ended with Japji Sahib, Nanak's morning poem. Your line was 38 stanzas, verse by verse. Did the first minute of today go to something that matters? Day twenty-two, and camp two: the stories.
screen: `JAPJI SAHIB — 38 STANZAS, VERSE BY VERSE.`

segments.voice: Punjab, in the spring of 1469. Wheat fields running flat to the horizon. A village of mud-brick houses called Talwandi, a day's walk or so from the city of Lahore. The local landlord is a Muslim named Rai Bular. His village accountant, the man who keeps the records of land and harvests, is a Hindu named Mehta Kalu. And in Kalu's house, his wife, Mata Tripta, is about to give birth to her second child. Nothing about this looks like the beginning of anything. No palace, no prophecy anyone's written down, no crowd outside. Just a family, a village, a baby. For the next weeks we'll tell his story. It starts right here.
screen: `PUNJAB, SPRING, 1469.` → `A VILLAGE CALLED TALWANDI.` → `A FAMILY, A VILLAGE, A BABY.`

segments.voice: The baby was Nanak. His father, Mehta Kalu, was a Khatri, from a caste of traders and record-keepers, a practical man who hoped his son would grow up to earn a respectable living. His mother, Mata Tripta, is remembered in Sikh tradition for her gentleness and her quiet faith in her unusual son. He had an older sister, Nanaki, and she gets her own day tomorrow. The janamsakhis, the life-stories you met on day eighteen, surround the birth with signs: a room filled with light, a midwife who said she'd never seen a child like this. Those are the stories people tell, and Sikhs tell them with joy. What we can say plainly is where and roughly when. Here's an honest wrinkle. The oldest accounts place his birth in the spring, in the month of Vaisakh. But Sikhs usually celebrate Guru Nanak's birthday at the full moon of Kartik, in October or November, following another early tradition. Scholars have argued about the date for a long time. Most Sikhs simply celebrate in the autumn, with lights and processions and all-night singing, and nobody's faith hangs on the calendar. And the village? Talwandi is now called Nankana Sahib, Nanak's town, and since 1947 it has been in Pakistan. A gurdwara stands on the spot where tradition says he was born. Every year thousands of Sikh pilgrims cross the border to visit it, and many of the local people who welcome them are Muslims. A boy born in a village with a Muslim landlord and a Hindu accountant. It fits, somehow, for the man who'd say there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

segments.voice: Settle, and think of the place you were born. If you know it, picture it: the town, the hospital, the house, the street. If you don't know much about it, picture what you imagine. Think of the people who were there: a mother, maybe a father, maybe others waiting. Nobody there knew what your life would be. Let yourself feel how small and ordinary that beginning was, and how much has grown from it. Stay with that place for a while. The bell holds the time.

23.title: The sister who saw first
23.hook: his older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was
23.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki as Guru Nanak's devoted older sister, often called the first to recognize him; a gurdwara in her memory stands in Sultanpur Lodhi.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: born at Talwandi, 1469, a baby in an ordinary village. Your line was every story starts somewhere small. Whose birthplace did you ask about? Day twenty-three.
screen: `BORN AT TALWANDI — SOMEWHERE SMALL.`

segments.voice: Think of the person who believed in you before you'd done anything to deserve it. Before the grades, the job, the good decisions. Maybe a grandmother who said you'd be something. A teacher who saw the thing you were too shy to show. An older sibling who told the others to leave you alone. Most of us have one, and most of us never properly thanked them. In the story of Guru Nanak, that person was his big sister. While the grown-ups in the village were worrying about the strange, dreamy boy who asked too many questions, she was watching him with a different kind of attention. Today: the sister who saw first.
screen: `BEFORE YOU'D DONE ANYTHING.` → `SOMEONE BELIEVED IN YOU.` → `FOR NANAK, HIS BIG SISTER.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nanaki, and Sikhs call her Bebe Nanaki, bebe being an affectionate word for an older sister or a respected woman. She was about five years older than Nanak. In the janamsakhis, the young Nanak is a puzzle to the people around him. He gives things away. He sits silent for hours. He asks the village priest and teacher questions they can't answer. His father, Mehta Kalu, loved him and worried about him constantly: how would this boy ever earn a living? Nanaki saw it differently. Sikh tradition remembers her as the first to recognize that her brother wasn't lost. He was found, in a way the others couldn't see yet. Some Sikhs go so far as to call her the first Sikh, the first follower of the Guru, though she was his sister before she was anything else. And she didn't only believe in him. She did something about it. Nanaki married a man named Jai Ram and moved to the town of Sultanpur, and when her brother was a young man, drifting and at odds with his father, she brought him there. Jai Ram helped find him work, and Nanak lived near her for years. Some of the most important moments in his life, which we'll reach in a few days, happened in Sultanpur, because she made room for him there. The sources don't tell us much about her own inner life, and it's worth saying so. What they do remember is the shape of her love: she saw him first, and she made space for what she saw.

24.title: The boy and the teacher
24.hook: tradition says young Nanak asked his village teacher what the letters really pointed to
24.howItsDone: Sikh children often hear this story when they begin learning Gurmukhi, and Guru Nanak's Patti, an acrostic on the alphabet in the Guru Granth Sahib, is sung in kirtan.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sister who saw first, Bebe Nanaki. Your line was someone saw you first. Did your one sentence reach them? Day twenty-four.
screen: `BEBE NANAKI — SOMEONE SAW YOU FIRST.`

segments.voice: Every parent knows the stage. The child who asks why. Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to go to bed? Why? And then why again, and again, until the grown-up runs out of answers and says because I said so. Most of us grow out of it. School teaches us the right answers, and we stop asking what's underneath them. The story goes that when Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher to learn his letters, so that one day he could keep accounts like his dad. The teacher wrote out the alphabet on a wooden board. And the boy asked a question that stopped the lesson. Today: the boy and the teacher.
screen: `WHY? AND WHY AGAIN.` → `SEVEN YEARS OLD, AT SCHOOL.` → `A QUESTION THAT STOPPED THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: In the janamsakhis, the village teacher, a pandha, writes the letters on a wooden writing board, a patti, and tells the boy to copy them. Nanak does. And then he asks: but what do they mean? Not what sound does this letter make. What does it point to? The teacher, used to children who just copied, doesn't know what to say. And the boy, the story goes, begins to explain: each letter can point you toward God. The first letter, toward the one who made everything. The next, toward truth. And so on, all through the alphabet, until the teacher bows to the student. That's the story. Here's what makes it more than a legend. In the Guru Granth Sahib there really is a poem by Guru Nanak called Patti, the writing board. It's an acrostic: it runs through the alphabet, and each letter opens a line about God and the soul. In paraphrase, one letter begins a line about the one who created the world and is master of all. Another warns the mind that it will have to give an account of itself. Many scholars think Nanak composed it as a grown man, and the janamsakhi set it back in his childhood, at the moment it seemed to belong. Either way, the question is his: what does this really point to? Tradition also says he later learned Persian from a Muslim teacher and studied Sanskrit texts too, so he wasn't against learning. He just wouldn't stop at the surface of it. The same boy who asked what the sacred thread was for, back on day three, asked what the alphabet was for. It's the question under his whole life.
screen: `A PANDHA, A WOODEN BOARD.` · `BUT WHAT DO THE LETTERS MEAN?` · `PATTI — AN ALPHABET POEM IN SCRIPTURE.` · `NOT AGAINST LEARNING. BENEATH IT.` · then, large: `ASK WHAT IT MEANS.`

segments.voice: Pick one word you use every day without thinking: home, friend, sorry, work, love. Let it sit in your mind. Then ask Nanak's question of it: what does this really point to? Don't rush for an answer. Let the word open slowly, like the letters on the teacher's board. Whatever comes, sit with it. The bell holds the time.

25.title: The cobra's shade
25.hook: tradition says that as he slept in the fields a cobra spread its hood to shade his face
25.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the cobra's shade as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's youth, and pilgrims to Nankana Sahib visit the gurdwara that tradition connects with it.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boy and the teacher, and the letters that point to God. Your line was ask what it means. What real question did you ask? Day twenty-five.
screen: `THE BOY AND THE TEACHER — ASK WHAT IT MEANS.`

segments.voice: A hot afternoon in Punjab. The kind of heat that flattens everything, when even the birds go quiet. Out in the pastures beyond Talwandi, a teenage boy has been sent to watch the family's buffaloes as they graze. It's a job for someone reliable, and his father has been hoping this will teach him some responsibility. But the boy has found a tree, and lain down beneath it, and in the heat he has fallen asleep. The afternoon wears on. The sun moves across the sky, and the tree's shade slides away from his face. And then, the story says, something came out of the grass.
screen: `A HOT AFTERNOON IN THE PASTURES.` → `THE BOY FALLS ASLEEP.` → `THE SHADE SLIDES AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the story the janamsakhis tell. As the sun crept onto the sleeping boy's face, a cobra slid up beside him, raised itself, and spread its hood wide, holding it over his face like a small umbrella, keeping him in shade. And at that moment Rai Bular, the Muslim landlord of Talwandi you met three days ago, came riding past. He saw the boy, the snake, the hood spread over the face, and he stopped. He didn't reach for a stick. He understood, the story says, that he was looking at someone the world itself was protecting. From that day, Rai Bular is remembered as one of the first to honor Nanak, and he defended the boy to his worried father more than once. Today a gurdwara in Nankana Sahib marks the place tradition connects with the story. Now, is it history? The sources don't let us say, and it's honest to admit that. Many Sikhs treasure it as a true event. Many others, and many historians, hear it the way you'd hear any sakhi: a story told to show something true. And what it shows is lovely. A cobra is the most dangerous creature in the field. In this story, the dangerous thing becomes the shelter. The world isn't only against the boy. Something out there, even something fierce, is looking after him. Sikhs speak of God as the protector who keeps the ones who remember, and the story makes that visible in a single picture: a hood, spread wide, over a sleeping face. Most of us have had a moment like that. Something that could have gone wrong, and didn't. A shelter we didn't arrange.

segments.voice: If you can, find some shade: a tree, a porch, the cool side of a room, or just close your eyes and imagine lying under that tree in Punjab. Let your body rest completely. Now think of one time you were protected without arranging it: a near miss, a stranger's help, a door that opened. Let yourself feel sheltered. Rest in the shade. The bell holds the time.

26.title: The true bargain
26.hook: sent with twenty rupees to strike a good deal, he feeds hungry holy men and comes home empty-handed
26.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of sacha sauda as an early sign of the langar and of Guru Nanak's teaching on sharing; Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Pakistan marks the place tradition connects with it.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cobra's shade, the hood spread over a sleeping face. Your line was something shelters you. What did you thank? Day twenty-six.
screen: `THE COBRA'S SHADE — SOMETHING SHELTERS YOU.`

segments.voice: Mehta Kalu has had enough. His son is a young man now, and he still hasn't shown the slightest interest in making money. The buffaloes wandered. The lessons turned into questions. So the father tries one more thing, the thing a practical man would try. He counts out twenty rupees, a real sum, puts it in his son's hand, and says: go to the market town. Buy something you can sell for more. Make a good deal. Bring back a profit. Show me you can do this. The son nods, takes the money, and sets off down the road. He does make a deal. Just not the one his father meant.
screen: `TWENTY RUPEES IN HIS HAND.` → `GO MAKE A GOOD DEAL.` → `NOT THE DEAL HIS FATHER MEANT.`

segments.voice: On the way, the story says, Nanak came across a group of holy men sitting by the road. Wandering ascetics, thin, quiet. He stopped and talked with them and found out they hadn't eaten in days. He looked at the twenty rupees. He thought about his father's words: make a good deal, a true one. And he went into the town and spent every coin on flour, lentils, butter and other food, brought it back and fed them all. Then he walked home with empty hands. Sacha sauda. Sacha means true. Sauda means a deal, a trade, a bargain. The true bargain. Nanak's answer to his father's instruction was that feeding the hungry was the most profitable deal anyone could make. You didn't lose twenty rupees; you traded them for something that doesn't run out. His father didn't see it that way. The janamsakhis say Mehta Kalu was furious, and some tellings say he struck his son. Others in the family, and Rai Bular, stepped in to calm him. It's an honest touch in the story: the Guru's family didn't always understand him, and it hurt. Sikhs often see in this moment an early seed of the langar you met on day eight: food for anyone hungry, bought with honest money, given freely. And there's a gurdwara today called Sacha Sauda, in Pakistan, on the spot where tradition says the holy men were fed. Notice the clever thing about the story, too. Nanak didn't disobey his father's words. He obeyed them more deeply than his father intended. Make a true deal, the father said. So he did.

segments.voice: Settle, and think about your money for a moment, without guilt. Where did it go this week? Coffee, rent, something online. Picture that twenty turning into a meal in their hands. Sit with how that deal feels. The bell holds the time.
Sacha sauda. The true bargain: twenty rupees traded for a meal for the hungry, the best deal Nanak could make.

27.title: The storehouse at Sultanpur
27.hook: weighing out grain as a storekeeper, he reaches thirteen, tera, which also means yours, and keeps saying it
27.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the tera story as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's years in Sultanpur Lodhi, and pilgrims visit the gurdwara there where tradition says the storehouse stood.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacha sauda, the true bargain, twenty rupees turned into a meal. Your line was the best bargain. Who did you feed? Day twenty-seven.
screen: `SACHA SAUDA — THE BEST BARGAIN.`

segments.voice: Remember Bebe Nanaki, who made room for her brother in the town of Sultanpur? Here's what happened when he got there. Her husband, Jai Ram, found him a steady job, the most respectable job the family could have hoped for. The local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi, needed someone honest to run the government storehouse, where grain collected as taxes was kept and handed out as wages and supplies. So the young man who'd come home empty-handed from the market was put in charge of the grain. By all accounts, he was very good at it. He married, started a family, and for a while it looked as if Mehta Kalu's son had finally settled down. Then came the day he started counting.
screen: `A STEADY JOB IN SULTANPUR.` → `THE GOVERNOR'S STOREHOUSE.` → `THEN HE STARTED COUNTING.`

segments.voice: The storehouse was called the modikhana, and a storekeeper measured out grain the old way: a scoop, a scale, counting out loud as each measure went into a customer's bag. One, two, three. In Punjabi: ik, do, tin. The story says one day Nanak was measuring out grain, counting as usual, up through ten, eleven, twelve. And then he reached thirteen. In Punjabi, thirteen is tera. And tera is also the Punjabi word for yours. As in: yours, God. All of it, yours. And he stopped counting. He just kept saying it. Tera. Tera. Tera. Scoop after scoop went into the bag, and every one was thirteen, every one was yours. It sounds like a man losing his mind at work. But look at what it says. Everything he was handing out, the grain, the scale, his own hands, the job, none of it was really his. It all belonged to God. So what was there to count? Someone, of course, complained to the governor that the storekeeper was giving the grain away. The accounts were checked. And the story says every grain was accounted for, and some tellings say there was even a surplus. In Sultanpur today there's a gurdwara where tradition says the storehouse stood, and weights said to be the ones he used are kept there. Here's the heart of it. Tera isn't a trick with numbers. It's a way of holding everything you have with open hands. My money, my house, my time become yours, lent to me for a while. And a person who really believes that tends to measure generously.
screen: `THE MODIKHANA — THE GRAIN STORE.` · `IK, DO, TIN... UP TO THIRTEEN.` · `TERA — THIRTEEN, AND YOURS.` · `THE ACCOUNTS CAME OUT RIGHT.` · then, large: `TERA, TERA, ALL YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let's count to thirteen together, slowly, one number per breath. Breathe in, and on the way out think one. Then two. Then three. Keep going, all the way to twelve. And when you reach thirteen, let it become tera, yours, and let everything you're holding today belong to something larger for a moment. Then just keep breathing, tera on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

28.title: Three days in the river
28.hook: he walks into the river Bein to bathe and is not seen for three days
28.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Bein river as the place where Guru Nanak's mission began; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Ber Sahib in Sultanpur Lodhi and many bathe in the river.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the modikhana, the storehouse where the counting stopped at thirteen. Your line was tera, tera, all yours. What did you hand over with open hands? Day twenty-eight, the end of the week.
screen: `MODIKHANA — TERA, TERA, ALL YOURS.`

segments.voice: Before dawn in Sultanpur. The storekeeper does what he does every morning: he walks down to the small river at the edge of town, the Bein, to bathe before the day begins. A servant waits on the bank with his clothes. Nanak steps into the water, and goes under. And doesn't come up. The servant waits. Then shouts. Then runs for help. People come with ropes and nets. The governor himself, the story says, has the river searched. Nothing. No body, no clothes, no trace. By evening the town has decided: the storekeeper has drowned. His sister grieves. A day passes. Then another. Today, three days in the river.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, THE RIVER BEIN.` → `HE GOES UNDER.` → `AND DOESN'T COME UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the first thing to say plainly. Nobody knows what happened in those three days. Nanak didn't describe it in any hymn that plainly tells the story. What we have is what the janamsakhis tell, and Sikhs treasure it. They say he was taken into the presence of God. There, he was given a cup of amrit, the nectar of immortality, and he drank it. And he was sent back with a charge: go into the world, remember the name, and teach others to remember it. After three days, on the third morning, he walked out of the river. Sikh tradition, in one of its early tellings, even says that in the presence of God the Mool Mantar was first spoken, the root verse you learned on days five and six. Not every telling says that. But many Sikhs hear the river as the moment Nanak's mission began. Historians generally think something decisive did happen around this time, when Nanak was about thirty, a profound experience that changed the direction of his life. What it was like from the inside, the sources leave in the water. And look at the week that led here. A baby born in Talwandi. A sister who saw first. A boy asking what the letters meant. A cobra's shade. A true bargain. A storekeeper saying tera. All of it building, quietly, until one morning he walked into a river and came out someone the whole town would have to reckon with. Today a gurdwara called Ber Sahib stands on the riverbank. The story says there's a jujube tree there that Nanak sat under.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED INSIDE.` · `A CUP OF AMRIT, AND A CHARGE.` · `SOMETHING DECISIVE, ABOUT AGE THIRTY.` · `A WEEK THAT BUILT TO THIS.` · then, large: `SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit by running water: a stream, a fountain, or just turn on a tap to a thin, steady trickle and sit beside it. Listen. Let the sound fill the room. Think of a time you went into something, a hard season, a trip, a loss, and came out different. You don't have to understand what happened. Just let the water run, and let yourself be changed a little by listening. The bell holds the time.
Three days in the river. Nanak disappears into the Bein at Sultanpur, and comes back, the stories say, with a mission.
screen: `THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: some come back changed. Today, go easy on someone who's come back from something different: a new parent, a grieving friend, a traveler. Next week: what he said when he came out. Day twenty-eight.
